Does biological constraints make neurons divide or share cognitive tasks?

Firing-rate vs wiring budgets and the task selectivity of excitatory units in multitask Dale RNNs

Published

November 9, 2026

1 Question

In the cortex both firing and wiring cost energy and space, so circuits are shaped by function and cost together. Recurrent networks trained on many cognitive tasks without any cost already form groups of units that serve particular tasks (Yang et al. 2019). What has not been separated is which cost pushes single neurons from mixed to task-specialized.

Question. In Dale’s-law RNNs trained on 20 cognitive tasks, does a firing-rate (metabolic) budget make excitatory (E) units carry fewer tasks than in unconstrained networks, and does a wiring budget do the same?

Expectation. A rate budget should narrow E units, because activity is paid for on every task a unit joins. A wiring budget limits who talks to whom, not how many tasks a unit’s activity varies with, so it should leave breadth about unchanged.

Order of events. Earlier exploratory analyses in the wider project suggested this expectation. For this study, the expectation, the metric and six pass/fail rules were then written down; two of the rules (2 and 5) were clarified in writing; and only then was the analysis run. Nothing in the rules was changed after results existed.

2 Approach

2.1 Networks

No new training: two existing sets of trained Dale’s-law RNNs, each with 256 units (204 E, 52 inhibitory, I) and 20 tasks. Networks in a condition differ only in their random seed, which is used below to identify them.

set training conditions × networks
main set 150 000 steps 4 × 5
second set (consistency check) 50 000 steps 4 × 12

The second set uses different budget values and a third of the training; it checks direction, not exact numbers. A network is feasible if it solves its worst task with at least 60 % accuracy (its min task accuracy ≥ 0.6).

2.2 Conditions and costs

  • Rate cost (also metabolic cost): the mean of the squared firing rate \(r^2\) over units, time steps and trials, with E and I units weighted by their share of the population. \(r\) is a unit’s rectified (ReLU) activity, so the cost is dimensionless. Reference: control networks 0.36–0.55.
  • Wiring cost: the mean absolute recurrent weight per synapse (an L1 norm divided by the number of synapses), with I weights rescaled so that E and I synapses count equally. Dimensionless. Reference: control networks 0.024–0.036.
  • Budget: a ceiling on a cost during training. The wiring budget is enforced exactly: after every training step the recurrent weights are projected back onto the ceiling if they exceed it. The rate budget is enforced by a multiplier.
  • Multiplier: a learned weight on the rate cost in the loss (a Lagrange multiplier). It grows while the rate cost is above its budget and shrinks while it is below, down to a floor of 10⁻⁶, which means “off”.
  • Binding: a budget binds if, at the end of training, the cost sits at the ceiling (for the rate budget: and its multiplier is above the floor). A budget set far above what the network uses is loose and never binds.
set condition rate budget wiring budget which budget binds
main control none none —
main rate-only (A3) 0.0011 1.0 (loose) rate
main wiring-only (B0) 10 (loose) 0.0054 wiring
main both budgets (C0) 0.0115 0.0044 wiring; rate cost sits at its ceiling, multiplier above the floor in 2 of 5 networks
second control none none —
second rate-limited 0.0037 0.0237 both (the wiring budget is just below control’s wiring cost)
second wiring-limited 0.0231 0.0020 wiring only (rate budget not binding)
second both budgets (knee) 0.0046 0.0025 both

The budgets act on the costs as measured on training batches; the costs reported in Results are measured after training on evaluation trials, which gives 1.3–2.0 times larger rate costs (see Limitations). The names in the “condition” column are used from here on.

2.3 Metric: task breadth

For each unit and task, the task variance is the variance of the unit’s rate across noise-free trials of that task, averaged over time after fixation onset (Yang et al. 2019).

  • Active unit: its total task variance (summed over tasks) is more than 1 % of the largest unit’s total in the same network.
  • Each unit’s 20 task variances are divided by its own maximum, so a quiet unit is not automatically “more selective”.
  • Breadth of a unit = the number of tasks whose normalized variance exceeds a threshold (0.5 unless stated; 1 = one task, 20 = all tasks).
  • E breadth of a network = the mean breadth over its active E units. The unit of analysis is the network, not the neuron.

2.4 Pre-registered rules

Each rule says when the expectation is wrong; each is tested on the main set at threshold 0.5 unless stated. “Below” means lower E breadth.

  1. No rate effect: the highest rate-only E breadth ≥ the lowest control E breadth.
  2. Threshold artefact: the separation of rule 1 breaks at threshold 0.3 or at 0.7.
  3. Accuracy, not budget: any rate-only network with min task accuracy ≥ the lowest control min task accuracy has an E breadth inside the control range.
  4. Population artefact: rate-only networks keep, on average, fewer than half as many active E units as control.
  5. Does not replicate: in the second set, mean rate-limited E breadth is not below mean control E breadth. Decided on feasible networks only; only 3 of 12 rate-limited networks are feasible, so this test is weak either way.
  6. Wiring does specialize: every wiring-only network’s E breadth is below the lowest control E breadth.

Registered claim (main set):

  • Rate effect. A binding rate budget narrows E task breadth: all 5 rate-only networks lie below all 5 control networks, at thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7.
  • No wiring effect. A moderate wiring budget alone does not narrow it: wiring-only networks sit at or above control (above every control network at threshold 0.3).
  • Not accuracy. Wiring-only networks are about as accurate as rate-only ones (overlapping ranges) yet stay broad, and the most accurate rate-only network, whose min task accuracy is inside the control range, is still narrow.
  • Second set. Rate-limited networks are below control too, but the registered test rests on 3 feasible networks.

Exploratory, not pre-registered: narrowing tracks realised firing rate. Every narrow condition has a far lower metabolic cost than control, whichever budget caused it:

  • In the second set, wiring-limited networks narrow as much as rate-limited ones although their rate budget does not bind (the multiplier stays at its floor in all 12). Their tight wiring budget (0.0020, against 0.0054 for wiring-only in the main set) lowers the metabolic cost, a mean squared rate, about 13-fold on its own.
  • In the main set’s both-budgets condition, the rate cost sits at its ceiling even though the multiplier is above the floor in only 2 of 5 networks.
  • Wiring-only, the one budgeted condition that stays broad, has a higher metabolic cost than control.

So the cleaner statement is about low firing, not about which budget is switched on. This was found after the rules were fixed and needs its own test.

4 Workflow

Everything from the trained networks to this document is one Snakemake pipeline (a workflow tool that reruns only the steps whose inputs changed) in a locked pixi environment (a pinned list of software versions). It runs on CPU; training ran elsewhere and is not part of it.

  • cmc/selectivity.py: the metric, the six rules, the figure and the report tables.
  • Pipeline steps (named “rules” by Snakemake; not the same as the six pre-registered rules): unit_table (one saved network at one threshold → a table with one row per unit) → summary (one row per network) → verdicts (pass/fail table), figure and tables (the two tables above). There are 204 unit tables: 68 networks (20 + 48) × 3 thresholds.
  • Checks, one per step: a ground-truth test on synthetic units with known breadth; boundary tests on the rule comparisons (a tie counts against the claim); agreement with an independent earlier implementation for all 20 main-set networks to 3 decimals; the plotted values read back from the figure; and a rebuild from scratch (3.5 min on 4 cores) with byte-identical outputs.

4.1 Reproduce

The trained networks are committed to the repository, so a clone contains everything needed. They are saved model files (“checkpoints”), one per network:

  • main set: runs/moo_zoom/dale_all_woutfree_fanin_4pt_5seed_150k/ (167 MB)
  • second set: runs/moo_zoom/dale_all_4pt_12seed_50k/ (241 MB; only the final checkpoints {condition}/seed_XX.pt are used, not the mid-training ones in step_025000/)

The folder names are the training runs’ internal names. The whole runs/ directory is about 1.7 GB, so the clone is large. The analysis lives on the branch agent-course.

git clone https://github.com/AtharvSuryawanshi/canonical_mc.git
cd canonical_mc
git checkout agent-course
pixi install        # locked environment from pixi.lock
pixi run test       # ground-truth tests
pixi run pipeline   # networks -> tables -> verdicts -> figure -> report tables
pixi run dag        # reports/dag.svg
pixi run report     # this document

5 How agents were used

Two documents steered the work: the spec, a written study plan with the question, metric and pass/fail rules, fixed before any result; and a progress file, a running log of what was done, the evidence for it, what comes next and open questions.

Setup. Three roles, with a human approving every change:

  • Planning agent: read the spec, the data and the code, and proposed a plan with one check per step. No edits until the human approved; the approved plan was written into the spec before any result.
  • Builder agent: the same session after approval. It built one step at a time, ran each step’s check, showed the output as evidence, and updated the progress file. It never committed: the human committed after reading each diff.
  • Reviewer agent: a separate agent with a fresh context and read-only tools (read, search, shell), asked to break three summary claims against the result files and the training logs.
stage delegated to an agent decided by the human checked by
question, expectation, pass/fail rules — written before any analysis; never edited —
plan reading the data, drafting steps and checks approval; clarifications of rules 2 and 5; which outputs are tracked plan fixed in the spec before results
metric code metric and tests — ground-truth tests; independent earlier implementation (20/20 networks)
rule code pass/fail logic the comparisons, checked side by side with the plan boundary tests (ties, closed ranges)
figure, tables plotting, generated tables panels, condition and set names plotted dots read back against the tables
reproducibility rebuild from scratch — checksums of every output, identical
review finding weaknesses in the claims accepting all 5 findings; revising the explanation builder re-ran the reviewer’s key numbers
commits, report text drafts every commit, every edit to the claim diff read before each commit

What the routine caught:

  • Infeasible second set. While planning, the agent read the second set’s metadata and found that only 3 of 12 rate-limited networks are feasible. This was recorded before any result, and rule 5 was clarified (feasible only, called weak either way) before it was computed.
  • Stray output commit. A per-unit table from the first test run was committed by hand. Per-unit tables are now regenerated rather than tracked, and only the network tables, pass/fail table and figure are committed.
  • A leaking reference. The first plan named the earlier implementation’s file and its expected value inside the spec. It was replaced by a pointer to the progress file, so the spec does not carry a number the pipeline is meant to reproduce.
  • A reviewer that broke the explanation. The reviewer accepted the registered result but showed that the stated reason (“where a wiring budget narrows, a rate budget is also active”) was wrong: the second set’s wiring-limited networks narrow with a rate budget that does not bind. All five of its findings were accepted. The pass/fail results did not change, the explanation did, and the firing-rate account is labelled exploratory.

6 Limitations

  • n = 5 per condition in the main set. Full separation of 5 vs 5 has an exact one-sided p ≈ 0.004; “all rate-only networks” describes these networks, not a population.
  • One level per budget. Wiring-only is a single, moderate wiring level; the second set shows a tighter one does narrow. The result is “a moderate wiring budget does not”, not “wiring never does”.
  • Weak consistency check. Most budgeted networks in the second set are infeasible, its budgets differ from the main set’s, and training is a third as long.
  • Population changes. Both-budgets (main set) and the second set’s wiring-limited and both-budgets conditions lose 11–23 % of their active E units; rule 4 tests this only for rate-only.
  • Mechanism. The rate cost is L2, which by itself favours spreading activity thinly, not concentrating it. Why low firing narrows tuning is not addressed here.
  • Metric choices. Breadth depends on the activity cut-off (1 %) and the normalization; the threshold was varied (0.3–0.7), the activity cut-off was not.
  • Cost measurement. The rate cost measured after training is 1.3–2.0 times the training-time value the budget acts on (rate-only: 0.0018–0.0022 against its 0.0011 budget). The ratio is similar in every budgeted condition, including wiring-only, where the rate budget is loose, and noise does not explain it (re-simulating one network with and without training noise changes the cost by 2 %). Its source was not identified; all comparisons use the after-training value.

7 Next steps

  • A wiring sweep with firing rate measured, to separate the wiring level from the firing rate it induces (the exploratory account predicts breadth follows firing rate across both budgets).
  • Matched-accuracy comparisons with more networks per condition.
  • Find the source of the gap between the training-time and after-training rate cost.
  • I units, reported but not analysed here (their breadth changes less than E’s).
